title: Mock Exam 21: Mountains, Glaciers & the Polar Regions

listeningParts.title: Booking a guided glacier walk
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones the visitor centre of a national park to book a guided walk on a glacier.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Icefield Discovery Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm planning a trip to the national park in August with my sister, and I'm interested in one of your guided glacier walks. Could you tell me a bit about them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. We run two guided walks on the glacier itself. The first is the Ice Explorer, which is a half-day trip. You spend about three hours on the ice, and it's suitable for anyone aged ten or over who can walk comfortably for a few hours. The second is the Glacier Discovery, which is a full day, roughly seven hours, and it goes much further up the glacier, towards the icefall.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Sorry, what's an icefall?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's a steep part of the glacier where the ice breaks up into huge blocks and deep cracks, which we call crevasses. You don't go into it, of course, but you get a fantastic view of it. The full-day walk is more demanding, so we ask that people are fit and have done some hill walking before.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We both do a lot of hiking at home, so I think the full day would be fine. How much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The Glacier Discovery is a hundred and sixty-five dollars per person. The half-day trip is ninety-five. The price includes a qualified guide, transport from the centre to the start of the trail, and all the specialist equipment.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: What kind of equipment do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Crampons, which are metal spikes that attach to your boots so you don't slip on the ice, as well as a helmet and a harness. You'll need your own boots, though. They have to be stiff mountain boots, because ordinary trainers or soft walking shoes won't hold crampons properly.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I've got proper boots, but my sister only has light walking shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's not a problem. We rent boots here at the centre for fifteen dollars a day. Just let us know her size in advance, so we can have a pair ready.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. And what else should we bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Layers of warm clothing, gloves and a hat, because it can be cold on the ice even in the middle of summer. And sunglasses are essential. The sunlight reflected off the ice is very strong, and without good sunglasses you can actually damage your eyes. Sun cream too, of course. We provide lunch on the full-day trip, but bring plenty of water.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Which days does the full-day walk run?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: In August it runs on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, and groups are limited to twelve people.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Could we book for Wednesday the fourteenth?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me just check. I'm sorry, the fourteenth is already fully booked. But there are still a few places on Friday the sixteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The sixteenth is fine. We're staying in the area for a whole week.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Can I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Rachel Dunmore. That's D-U-N-M-O-R-E.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thanks, Rachel. Now, on the day, please be at the centre by seven forty-five. The bus leaves at eight o'clock sharp, and it's about a forty-minute drive to the trailhead.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there parking at the centre?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a large car park behind the building, and it's free for people on our tours. Just leave a note with your booking reference on the dashboard so the attendant knows you're with us.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what happens if the weather is bad?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Our guides make the decision early on the morning of the trip. If there's heavy rain, strong wind or fog, we cancel, because it isn't safe on the ice when you can't see the crevasses clearly. In that case, you can either have a full refund or move to another date.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That seems fair. Do we need to pay everything now?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No, we take a deposit of fifty dollars per person to hold the places, and the rest is paid when you arrive. I can take the deposit over the phone by card if you like.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Let's do that. Oh, and one more thing. Is there anything to do at the centre if we arrive early?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a small exhibition about how the glacier has changed over the last hundred years or so. There are photographs taken in the 1920s that show the ice reaching almost down to where the car park is now. Today, the front of the glacier is about two kilometres further up the valley, so it's quite a striking comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds really interesting. Thanks very much for your help, Megan.

listeningParts.title: A welcome talk at a mountain national park
listeningParts.contextDescription: A park ranger gives an evening talk to visitors at a national park visitor centre.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Ben Arran National Park. I'm Fiona, one of the park rangers, and I'm going to spend the next twenty minutes or so telling you a little about the park, how to stay safe in the mountains, and some of the trails and huts you can use during your stay.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The park was established in 1987, and it covers just over nine hundred square kilometres. It contains eleven peaks over a thousand metres high, which makes it one of the most popular areas for hill walking in the country. Around three hundred thousand people visit each year, most of them between May and September. That brings a lot of money into the local villages, but it also causes problems. The biggest one, perhaps surprisingly, isn't litter, because most visitors are very good about taking it home. It's the erosion of the paths. When a path gets muddy, people walk around the edges, and the path gets wider and wider until whole hillsides are scarred. So please stay on the stone surface, even when it's wet.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, safety. The weather in the mountains can change remarkably quickly. It's quite common to set off in sunshine and find yourself in thick cloud an hour later, and the temperature at the summits is usually around eight to ten degrees lower than it is down here in the valley. So whatever the forecast says, carry waterproofs and an extra warm layer. And please don't rely only on your phone for navigation. Batteries run down fast in the cold, and in many parts of the park there's no signal at all. We strongly recommend carrying a paper map and a compass, and knowing how to use them. In fact, we run free map-reading sessions here at the visitor centre every Saturday morning, and you're all very welcome to come along.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Before you set off on a longer walk, leave details of your route and the time you expect to be back with someone, either a friend or the staff at your accommodation. If something does go wrong, call the emergency number and ask for the police, and then for mountain rescue. The rescue teams here are all volunteers, and they're called out around sixty times a year. A surprising number of those call-outs aren't because of injuries at all, but because walkers have simply got lost or been caught out by darkness. So check what time the sun sets and give yourself plenty of time to get down.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about four routes and huts I'd particularly like to mention. The Lochside Trail is the easiest. It's a flat circuit of about eight kilometres around the loch, and it's the only route in the park that's suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs along most of its length. There's a café at the halfway point, which is open from Easter until the end of October.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The Corrie Path is a steeper walk up into a corrie, which is a bowl-shaped hollow carved out by a glacier during the last ice age. At the top there's a small lake, and in early summer it's one of the best places in the park to see alpine flowers. The path is steep and rocky in places, so I wouldn't recommend it for young children.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Then there's Stag Ridge, which is the classic route to the highest summit. It's a long day, eight hours or more, and there's a narrow section near the top where you'll need to use your hands to climb over the rocks. In winter conditions it should only be attempted by people with an ice axe and crampons and the experience to use them. We've had several serious accidents there involving people who underestimated it.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Finally, for those of you who'd like to stay overnight in the hills, there's Glenbeg Hut. It's a simple stone shelter, the kind of building known in Scotland as a bothy. It's free to use and you don't need to book, but there's no electricity or running water, so you'll need to bring your own sleeping bag and stove. Please carry all your rubbish out with you. The hut is looked after by a charity whose members are all volunteers, so if you use it, do consider making a donation. Glenbeg is also the best spot in the park for seeing red deer, especially at dawn.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Before I finish, a quick word about wildlife. In spring, several kinds of bird lay their eggs on the ground on the open hillsides, so between April and July we ask dog owners to keep their dogs on a short lead. And please don't feed the deer near the car parks. It encourages them to come close to the roads, and sadly several are hit by cars every year. Right, I'll be at the information desk for the next half hour if you have any questions, and you can pick up a free trail map on your way out.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on shrinking mountain glaciers
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Jake and Amira, discuss their presentation on mountain glaciers with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, Jake, Amira. So, you wanted to talk about your presentation on mountain glaciers. How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: We've done most of the research, and we've agreed on the structure. We want to start with the evidence that glaciers are shrinking, then look at why it matters for people living downstream, and finish with some of the ways communities are responding.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds logical. What evidence are you planning to use for the first part?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: We were going to show a lot of graphs of measurements, but we decided that might be a bit dry for the audience. So instead we're going to open with repeat photography. That's where you take a photo from exactly the same spot as an old historical photograph, so you can compare them directly. There are some amazing pairs from the Alps, where you can see a valley full of ice in about 1900 and then just bare rock today.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Those images are very powerful. But make sure you also give some numbers, so it doesn't seem like you're relying on a few dramatic pictures.

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: Yes, we'll include figures from the Swiss monitoring network. Switzerland has some of the best long-term records in the world, and their data show that Swiss glaciers lost around ten per cent of their total volume in just two years, 2022 and 2023. Both years had very hot summers and not much snow in the winter before.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a striking figure. Are you going to mention Iceland as well?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Yes, we want to talk about Okjökull. It was officially declared dead in 2014, because it had become too thin to move under its own weight, which is what defines a glacier. In 2019 people held a kind of funeral and put up a memorial plaque, with a message addressed to the future. We thought it would make a memorable ending to the first section.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, the second part, why it matters. What have you found?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: The main issue is water supply. In places like the Himalayas and the Andes, millions of people depend on rivers that are partly fed by meltwater, especially in the dry season. What surprised me was the idea of peak water. As glaciers melt faster, rivers actually get more water at first, so things can look fine. But once the glaciers get small enough, the amount of meltwater starts to fall, and that's when the shortages begin.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, it's a very counterintuitive idea, so you'll need to explain it carefully. A simple diagram might help.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: I'll draw one. The other big risk we're covering is floods from glacial lakes. When a glacier retreats, meltwater often collects behind the loose rock and ice that the glacier left behind. These natural dams can suddenly fail, and the flood can travel a long way down the valley.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the final section, on responses?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: We've got two examples. One is in Switzerland, at the Rhône Glacier, where people cover part of the ice with large white sheets in summer to reflect sunlight and slow down the melting. It works on a small scale, near a tourist ice cave, but it's far too expensive to use on whole glaciers, so we want to be clear that it's not a real solution.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: The other is the ice stupas in Ladakh, in northern India. An engineer called Sonam Wangchuk developed a way of piping stream water down from higher up and spraying it into the freezing winter air, so it builds up into tall cones of ice. Because the cone shape has a small surface area for its volume, the ice melts slowly in spring, just when farmers need water for their crops.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a lovely example, because it's cheap and locally designed. How long is the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Jake
dialogue.text: Twenty minutes, plus five minutes for questions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then I'd suggest cutting back the first section a little. Audiences generally accept that glaciers are shrinking, so spend more time on the consequences and responses, which are less familiar. And please send me your slides by Thursday, so I can give you feedback before the session on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Okay, we'll do that. Thanks.

listeningParts.title: How glaciers shape the land
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a physical geography course on how glaciers erode and deposit material, and the landforms they leave behind.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at glaciers, and in particular at the way they shape the landscape. Even if you've never seen a glacier, you've almost certainly seen landscapes created by them, because during the last ice age, ice covered much of northern Europe and North America.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with how a glacier forms. A glacier develops wherever more snow falls in winter than melts in summer, so that snow builds up year after year. As new layers are added, the older snow underneath is compressed. The snowflakes lose their delicate shape and become rounded grains, forming a dense material called firn, which is halfway between snow and ice. Over many years, as the pressure increases, the air spaces are squeezed out and the firn turns into solid glacial ice.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Once the ice is thick enough, it begins to move downhill under its own weight. It does this in two main ways. First, the ice itself deforms slowly, rather like very stiff toothpaste. Second, in many glaciers, the whole mass of ice slides over the rock beneath it on a thin layer of meltwater. Most glaciers move at somewhere between a few centimetres and a few metres a day, although some fast-flowing glaciers in Greenland can travel many kilometres in a year.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: As they move, glaciers erode the land, mainly through two processes. The first is called plucking. Meltwater seeps into cracks in the rock under the glacier and then freezes onto it, so that when the ice moves on, it pulls away blocks of rock. The second process is abrasion. Rocks frozen into the bottom of the glacier scrape across the bedrock, a bit like a giant sheet of sandpaper. This leaves long, parallel scratches on the rock surface, which are called striations. They're very useful to geologists, because they show the direction in which the ice was moving.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now let's look at the landforms that result. High in the mountains, glaciers often begin in hollows on the side of a mountain. Over thousands of years, the ice deepens these into steep-sided, bowl-shaped basins called cirques. In Scotland they're known as corries, and in Wales as cwms. When the ice melts, a cirque often contains a small lake, which is called a tarn. Where two cirques form back to back, the ridge between them is worn into a sharp, narrow edge called an arête. And where three or more cirques cut into a single mountain, the result can be a pyramidal peak. The most famous example is the Matterhorn, on the border between Switzerland and Italy.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Further down, glaciers flowing along river valleys change their shape completely. Rivers tend to cut narrow V-shaped valleys, but a glacier fills the whole valley and erodes its sides as well as its floor, producing a wide valley with steep sides and a flat bottom, which we call U-shaped. Smaller side glaciers don't erode as deeply as the main glacier, so when the ice disappears, their valleys are left high above the main valley floor. These are known as hanging valleys, and they're often marked by spectacular waterfalls, like those in Yosemite in California. Along some coastlines, glacial valleys were later flooded by the sea when sea levels rose at the end of the ice age. These are fjords, and the best-known examples are in Norway, where the longest is over two hundred kilometres long.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Glaciers don't only remove material; they also deposit it. All the rock they carry is eventually dropped, often as an unsorted mix of clay, sand and boulders. Ridges of this material are called moraines, and the one at the furthest point the ice reached is known as the terminal moraine. Under the ice, the material can be shaped into smooth, oval hills called drumlins. They're often described as looking like an egg cut in half lengthways, and they usually occur in groups, with their long axis pointing in the direction of ice flow.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, erratics. These are boulders that the ice has carried far from where they originally formed, sometimes hundreds of kilometres, so they're a completely different type of rock from the ground they rest on. In the nineteenth century, erratics were an important part of the evidence used by the Swiss-born scientist Louis Agassiz to argue that large parts of Europe had once been covered by ice. Next week, we'll look at how these features are used to reconstruct past climates.

readingPassages.title: The race to the South Pole
paragraphs: In the first decade of the twentieth century, the South Pole was one of the last great geographical prizes still unclaimed. By 1910 two expeditions were preparing to reach it: a British party led by Robert Falcon Scott, a Royal Navy officer, and a Norwegian party led by Roald Amundsen. Their contrasting fortunes have been debated for more than a century, and the story remains one of the most closely studied episodes in the history of exploration.

Amundsen had not originally intended to go south at all. His plan was to drift across the Arctic Ocean in the Fram, the ship previously used by the Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, and to reach the North Pole. In 1909, however, the Americans Frederick Cook and Robert Peary each announced that they had already reached it. Fearing that his sponsors would lose interest, Amundsen quietly changed his destination, revealing the new plan to most of his crew only when the ship stopped at the island of Madeira. From there he sent a brief telegram informing Scott that the Fram was heading for Antarctica.

Scott, by contrast, was an experienced Antarctic leader. He had commanded the Discovery expedition of 1901 to 1904, and his new expedition, which sailed in the Terra Nova, had substantial scientific aims as well as the goal of reaching the Pole. Its members studied geology, meteorology, biology and magnetism, and during the winter of 1911 three of them made a dangerous journey in almost total darkness to collect the eggs of emperor penguins, an episode later described by one of them, Apsley Cherry-Garrard, in his book The Worst Journey in the World.

The two leaders made very different choices about transport. Amundsen relied entirely on dogs and skis. He had spent long periods in the Canadian Arctic during his earlier voyage through the Northwest Passage, and had learned from the Netsilik Inuit how to drive dogs and how to dress in loose fur clothing. Scott used a mixture of motor sledges, ponies and dogs, but planned for his men to pull the sledges themselves for much of the route. The motor sledges broke down early, and the ponies, which suffered badly in the cold, had to be shot.

Amundsen set out from his base at the Bay of Whales in October 1911 with four companions and around fifty dogs. He planned from the outset to kill some of the dogs on the way and use them as food for the remaining animals and the men, which allowed his loads to become lighter as the journey progressed. The Norwegians reached the Pole on 14 December 1911. Before leaving, they put up a small tent and left a letter inside, asking Scott to deliver it to the King of Norway if they did not survive the return journey.

Scott's final party of five reached the Pole on 17 January 1912, only to find the Norwegian tent. 'Great God! this is an awful place,' Scott wrote in his diary. The return journey became a disaster. Edgar Evans died in February after a fall, and in March Lawrence Oates, whose feet were severely frostbitten, walked out of the tent into a blizzard, apparently so as not to slow down his companions. Scott, Edward Wilson and Henry Bowers died in their tent around the end of March, only about eighteen kilometres from a large store of food and fuel. Their bodies were found by a search party in November 1912.

Among the belongings recovered with them were about sixteen kilograms of rock samples, which the men had continued to haul even as they grew weaker. These included fossils of a plant called Glossopteris, which showed that Antarctica had once supported forests and a much warmer climate. The same plant had already been found in South America, Africa, India and Australia, and such fossils later became part of the evidence that the continents had once been joined together.

For decades after his death, Scott was celebrated in Britain as a tragic hero. In 1979, however, the writer Roland Huntford published a highly critical account, arguing that Scott's poor planning had cost the lives of his men. More recently, the atmospheric scientist Susan Solomon has used weather records to argue that the temperatures the party faced in March 1912 were unusually low, and that bad luck with the weather played a larger part than earlier critics allowed. Amundsen himself continued to explore, and in 1926 he flew over the North Pole in an airship. He died in 1928 when his aircraft disappeared during a rescue mission in the Arctic.

readingPassages.title: Archives in the ice
paragraphs: The great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica are, in a sense, the largest libraries on Earth. Each year, snow falls on their surfaces and is buried by the snow of the following year, so that the ice forms a stack of layers stretching back hundreds of thousands of years. By drilling down through these layers and extracting long cylinders of ice, known as cores, scientists can read a detailed record of the Earth's past climate, and even of the air that our ancestors breathed.

The key to this record lies in the way snow turns into ice. Near the surface, fresh snow is loose and full of air. As it is buried, it is slowly compressed into a granular material called firn, through which air can still move. Only at a depth of roughly fifty to a hundred metres do the passages close completely, sealing small bubbles of air inside the ice. Because this happens well below the surface, the air in a bubble is always somewhat younger than the ice that surrounds it, a difference that can amount to thousands of years in places where very little snow falls.

To find out how warm or cold it was when the snow fell, scientists measure the chemistry of the water itself. Water molecules contain either a common, lighter form of oxygen or a rarer, heavier one. In the 1950s the Danish scientist Willi Dansgaard showed that the proportion of the heavier form in rain and snow depends closely on the temperature at which it formed: the colder the air, the less of the heavy form the snow contains. By measuring this ratio layer by layer, researchers can build up a continuous record of past temperatures.

Obtaining the cores has required remarkable feats of engineering. In 1966, at Camp Century, a United States military base built inside the Greenland ice sheet, a drill reached the bedrock for the first time, recovering a core nearly 1,400 metres long. Later projects went much deeper. At the Russian Vostok station in East Antarctica, drilling in the 1990s produced a core more than three and a half kilometres long, covering about 420,000 years. A European project at a site called Dome C then extended the record to around 800,000 years.

The results of this work have been profound. The Antarctic cores show that, over the past 800,000 years, the Earth has swung repeatedly between long, cold glacial periods and shorter, warmer interglacials. Throughout these cycles, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the trapped air rose and fell closely in step with temperature, varying between roughly 180 parts per million in the coldest periods and about 300 in the warmest. Today, the figure is above 420, far outside the range found anywhere in the ice.

Cores from Greenland revealed something equally significant. Two cores drilled in the early 1990s, one by a European team and one by an American team, showed that during the last glacial period the climate of Greenland had repeatedly jumped by ten degrees Celsius or more within a few decades. Until then, many scientists had assumed that major climate changes took thousands of years. The discovery that the climate system could change so abruptly forced a fundamental rethink, and it continues to shape how researchers assess the risks of present-day warming.

The ice also preserves a record of individual events. Large volcanic eruptions leave layers of sulphuric acid that can be detected by passing an electric current along the core, and these layers help scientists to date the ice precisely. Human activity has left its mark too. Greenland ice contains traces of lead released by mining and smelting in the Roman period, and layers from the 1950s and 1960s contain radioactive material from nuclear weapons tests, which provides a convenient marker for dating recent snow.

Two challenges now face the field. The first is to find even older ice. About a million years ago, the rhythm of the ice ages changed, with cycles lengthening from about 41,000 years to roughly 100,000, and nobody yet knows why. Recovering ice from this period, which requires finding places where the deepest layers have not melted or been disturbed, could help to answer the question. The second challenge is more urgent: many mountain glaciers, which hold their own valuable records, are melting so quickly that their archives may be lost. A project called Ice Memory has therefore begun collecting cores from threatened glaciers, such as those in the Alps, to be stored in a cave dug into the snow in Antarctica for future generations of scientists.

readingPassages.title: A continent for peace and science
paragraphs: Antarctica is unlike any other place on Earth. Covering around fourteen million square kilometres, it is almost twice the size of Australia, yet it has no permanent population. The only residents are a few thousand scientists and support staff in summer, falling to around a thousand in the long, dark winter. Equally unusual is the way it is governed. No single country controls Antarctica; instead, it is managed under an international agreement that has, remarkably, survived for more than sixty years.

This was not inevitable. In the first half of the twentieth century, seven countries made formal claims to parts of the continent: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom. Most claims took the form of wedge-shaped sectors meeting at the South Pole, and three of them, those of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom, overlap on the Antarctic Peninsula. Meanwhile, the United States and the Soviet Union made no claims of their own but refused to recognise anyone else's, and reserved the right to make claims in the future.

The turning point came with the International Geophysical Year of 1957 to 1958, an eighteen-month programme of scientific cooperation during which twelve countries established dozens of research stations in Antarctica. Building on this spirit, the same twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington on 1 December 1959, and it came into force in 1961. The treaty states that Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only, guarantees freedom of scientific research, and bans nuclear explosions and the disposal of radioactive waste. Any station can be inspected by observers from other treaty nations at any time. Most cleverly, the treaty neither accepts nor rejects existing territorial claims, but simply freezes them, so that no activity carried out while it is in force can strengthen or weaken a claim. In my view, this was a stroke of genius: by setting aside a dispute that could not be solved, it allowed cooperation on everything else.

Since then, the system has grown considerably. More than fifty countries are now parties to the treaty, although only those that carry out substantial scientific research in Antarctica become Consultative Parties with the right to take part in decisions. These decisions are made by consensus, meaning that every Consultative Party must agree. The treaty has also been extended by further agreements, together known as the Antarctic Treaty System.

The most important of these concerns mining. During the 1980s, treaty nations negotiated a convention that would have allowed mineral resources to be exploited under strict controls. In 1989, however, Australia and France announced that they would not sign it, arguing instead for complete protection, and the convention was abandoned. In its place came the Protocol on Environmental Protection, signed in Madrid in 1991, which came into force in 1998. It designates Antarctica as a natural reserve devoted to peace and science, and prohibits all activity relating to mineral resources other than scientific research. It is often claimed that this ban will expire in 2048. This is a misunderstanding. After that date, any Consultative Party may request a conference to review the protocol, but lifting the ban would still require broad agreement and a binding system to regulate mining, which seems most unlikely.

The surrounding ocean is managed by another body, the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, established in the early 1980s, largely in response to concern about the growing harvest of krill. These small crustaceans are the main food of many whales, seals and penguins, and the commission was one of the first international bodies to manage fishing with the needs of the whole ecosystem in mind. In 2016 it created a vast marine protected area in the Ross Sea. Since then, however, proposals for further protected areas have been blocked for years because a small number of members objected. I believe this shows the weakness of consensus as well as its strength: it gives every member a sense of ownership, but it also allows a single country to prevent action that most others regard as necessary.

Tourism presents a newer challenge. In recent seasons, more than a hundred thousand visitors a year have travelled to Antarctica, most of them on cruise ships to the Antarctic Peninsula. Much of the industry is self-regulated through the International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators, founded in 1991. Under guidelines adopted by the industry and the treaty nations, ships carrying more than five hundred passengers may not land them at all, and no more than a hundred people may be ashore at any one site at the same time. Some campaigners argue that tourism should be banned altogether. I do not believe that a ban would be right. Visitors who have seen Antarctica for themselves often become its strongest defenders, and the industry's rules have so far been largely respected. What is needed is not prohibition but firmer limits that are legally binding, rather than voluntary.

The treaty system now faces pressures its founders could not have imagined, from a warming climate to growing global demand for resources and rising tensions between major powers. Some observers doubt whether an agreement made in 1959 can survive them. In my view, such pessimism is premature. The treaty has already outlasted the Cold War that shaped it, and it has adapted repeatedly when the need arose. Its greatest achievement may be the simplest one: for more than six decades, an entire continent has been devoted to peace and science, and no shot has been fired over it in anger.
